lessons.title: Sweeteners: Sugar, HFCS, and Artificial Sweeteners
lessons.body:
Sweeteners give soft drinks their sweetness and body. In Africa, the most common is white refined sugar (sucrose) from cane or beet. It comes in 50 kg bags. For a 500 ml bottle of soda, you typically need 50â60 g of sugar to reach 10â12% sweetness. That is about 10â12 Brix. Sugar also adds mouthfeel and helps preserve the drink. Store sugar in a dry place; damp sugar clumps and can carry mould.

High-fructose corn syrup (HFCS) is a liquid sweetener made from maize starch. It is cheaper than sugar in some countries and easier to blend. HFCS 55 (55% fructose) is common in colas. It is about 1.3 times sweeter than sugar, so you use less. However, HFCS is not available everywhere in Africa. If you cannot get it, stick to sugar. HFCS must be stored in clean, sealed drums away from heat.

Artificial sweeteners like aspartame, sucralose, and stevia are used in diet or low-calorie drinks. Aspartame is 200 times sweeter than sugar, so you need only 0.5 g per litre for the same sweetness as 100 g sugar. But aspartame breaks down at high temperatures and loses sweetness over time. Use it in cold-filled drinks only. Sucralose is more stable and 600 times sweeter. Stevia is natural but has a bitter aftertaste; blend it with a little sugar to mask that.

When formulating, always calculate sweetness equivalence. For example, to replace 100 g sugar per litre with aspartame: 100 g / 200 = 0.5 g aspartame. But artificial sweeteners lack bulk, so you may need bulking agents like maltodextrin or erythritol to improve mouthfeel. Also check local regulations: some countries restrict certain sweeteners. Always label accurately. For a small-scale producer, start with sugar because it is familiar and available. Experiment with a 10 Brix solution first, then adjust to taste.

lessons.title: Acidulants: Citric, Phosphoric, and Malic Acid
lessons.body:
Acidulants give soft drinks tartness, balance sweetness, and act as preservatives. The three main ones are citric, phosphoric, and malic acid. Citric acid is the most common. It is a white powder with a sharp, citrus taste. It comes from citrus fruits or fermentation. Use 0.5â2 g per litre for a typical fruit soda. Citric acid is very soluble in water. It also chelates metals, helping prevent off-flavours. Store it in a sealed container; it absorbs moisture.

Phosphoric acid is a clear liquid or crystals. It gives cola its distinctive tang. Use 0.5â1 ml per litre of 75% phosphoric acid solution. It is stronger than citric acid and has a flatter, less fruity taste. Phosphoric acid is corrosive; handle with gloves and goggles. Always add acid to water, never water to acid. It can also leach calcium from bones if consumed excessively, so use in moderation.

Malic acid is found in apples and gives a smooth, sour taste. It is less sharp than citric acid. Use 0.5â1.5 g per litre. Malic acid works well in fruit-flavoured drinks, especially apple and strawberry. It is more expensive and less available in Africa, so many producers blend it with citric acid. A common blend is 70% citric acid and 30% malic acid for a rounder flavour.

When adding acids, always dissolve them in a small amount of water first, then add to the batch. Add acids after sugar and before flavour. Too much acid makes the drink unpalatable and can cause stomach upset. Too little makes it taste flat. Use a pH meter or pH strips to check. Target pH 2.5â3.5 for most soft drinks. For a 1000 L batch, start with 1 kg citric acid, taste, and adjust. Always keep a record of your acid additions for consistency.

lessons.title: Flavorings: Natural and Synthetic
lessons.body:
Flavourings are what make a soft drink taste like cola, orange, or pineapple. They come as natural extracts, essential oils, or synthetic flavour compounds. Natural flavours are extracted from plants, fruits, or spices. For example, vanilla from vanilla beans, lemon from lemon peel oil, and ginger from ginger root. In Africa, you can make your own extracts by soaking chopped fruit or spices in high-proof alcohol (like vodka) for 2â4 weeks, then filtering. But natural flavours are often weak, expensive, and vary in strength.

Synthetic flavours are chemically identical to natural ones but made in a lab. They are cheaper, stronger, and consistent. Common ones include ethyl vanillin (vanilla), limonene (citrus), and cinnamaldehyde (cinnamon). For a cola, you need a blend of oils: orange, lemon, nutmeg, cinnamon, and vanilla. You can buy pre-made cola flavour concentrate from suppliers. For a small producer, buying concentrated flavours is easier than blending your own.

Dosage varies. A typical flavour concentrate is used at 0.1â0.5% of the final drink. That means for 100 L, use 100â500 ml of flavour. Always add flavour after sugar and acid, and mix well. Flavour oils do not dissolve in water; you need an emulsifier like gum arabic or polysorbate 80. Mix 1 part flavour oil with 1 part emulsifier, then add to the batch. Otherwise, the oil will float and give inconsistent taste.

Store flavours in dark glass bottles away from light and heat. Synthetic flavours last longer than natural ones. When starting, buy a few small samples and test them in 1 L batches. Keep notes on which brand and dosage you like. Remember, flavour is the most expensive ingredient per litre, so measure carefully. Never add flavour to hot liquid; heat drives off volatile compounds. Add at room temperature.

lessons.title: Colorants: Natural and Artificial
lessons.body:
Colorants make soft drinks visually appealing. Without them, orange soda would look like water. Natural colorants come from plants, insects, or minerals. Common ones: caramel colour (from heated sugar) for colas, anthocyanins (from red cabbage, berries) for reds and purples, carotenoids (from carrots, palm oil) for yellows and oranges, and chlorophyll (from greens) for green. Natural colours are safe but often fade with light, heat, or acid. They also add flavour notes. For example, beetroot juice gives a red colour but also an earthy taste.

Artificial colorants are synthetic dyes. They are bright, stable, and cheap. Examples: Tartrazine (Yellow 5), Sunset Yellow (Yellow 6), Allura Red (Red 40), Brilliant Blue (Blue 1). In many African countries, these are allowed but with limits. For instance, the maximum level for Tartrazine in soft drinks is often 100 mg per litre. Always check your national food safety regulations. Some artificial colours have been linked to hyperactivity in children, so some markets prefer natural.

To use colorants, first dissolve them in a small amount of water. Artificial dyes are very concentrated: 1 g can colour 1000 L. So make a stock solution: 1 g dye in 1 L water, then use 1 ml of that stock per litre of drink. Natural colours are weaker; you may need 5â20 ml per litre of liquid extract. Add colour after flavour, and mix gently to avoid foaming.

Test the colour in a clear glass against a white background. Aim for a shade that matches your target market. For example, a bright orange for Fanta-style, or a deep brown for cola. Keep records of your colour dosage. If using natural colours, store them in the fridge and use within a few weeks. Artificial colours last for months if kept dry. Always label your product with the colour name, especially if it is artificial.

lessons.title: Preservatives and Antioxidants
lessons.body:
Preservatives stop mould, yeast, and bacteria from spoiling your drink. Antioxidants stop fats and flavours from going rancid. In soft drinks, the main preservatives are sodium benzoate and potassium sorbate. They work best together. Sodium benzoate is effective in acidic drinks (pH below 4.5). Use 150â200 mg per litre. Potassium sorbate works over a wider pH range and prevents yeast and mould. Use 200â300 mg per litre. Combine them: 100 mg sodium benzoate + 150 mg potassium sorbate per litre gives good protection.

You must dissolve preservatives fully. Add them after sugar and acid, but before flavour. They work better when the drink is cold and the pH is low. If your drink is not acidic (pH above 4.5), benzoate is useless. In that case, you must rely on pasteurisation or refrigeration. Also, benzoate can form benzene (a carcinogen) if vitamin C is present. So do not add both. If you use vitamin C as an antioxidant, use potassium sorbate instead.

Antioxidants like ascorbic acid (vitamin C) protect colours and flavours from oxygen. Use 100â200 mg per litre. But ascorbic acid is also a nutrient, so it can feed microbes if not preserved properly. For natural colours, add 50 mg per litre of ascorbic acid to slow fading. Another antioxidant is EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid), which binds metals. Use 20â50 mg per litre. EDTA is not allowed in some countries, so check.

Always store preservatives in sealed containers away from moisture. Weigh accurately: a 0.01 g scale is needed. For a 100 L batch, 15 g sodium benzoate and 20 g potassium sorbate. Dissolve each separately in warm water, then add. Test your final drink for pH and taste. Preservatives can add a slight bitter or metallic taste if overdosed. Keep records. For small-scale production, you can also pasteurise at 85Â°C for 15 minutes and skip preservatives, but then you need refrigeration after opening.

lessons.title: Formulation Calculations and Brix Measurement
lessons.body:
Formulation is about getting the right balance of sugar, acid, flavour, and water. The key measurement is Brix, which tells you how much dissolved solids (mostly sugar) are in the drink. You measure Brix with a refractometer or a hydrometer. A refractometer is a small handheld device; put a drop of your drink on the glass, close the lid, and look through the eyepiece. The scale shows Brix. For a typical soft drink, target 10â12 Brix. For diet drinks, Brix will be near 0 because artificial sweeteners add little solids.

To calculate how much sugar to add, use this formula: Sugar (g) = (Target Brix Ã Volume (L)) / (100 - Target Brix) Ã 100. Wait, that's for syrup. Simpler: For a 100 L batch at 10 Brix, you need 10 kg sugar per 100 L. Because 10 Brix means 10 g sugar per 100 g solution. Since 1 L water weighs 1 kg, 100 L water = 100 kg. So 10% of 100 kg = 10 kg sugar. But adding sugar increases volume, so you actually need a bit less water. For small batches, just add 10 kg sugar to 90 L water, then top up to 100 L. That gives approximately 10 Brix.

Always measure Brix after mixing. If it's too low, add sugar. If too high, add water. Keep a record. For acid, target pH 2.5â3.5. Use a pH meter or strips. For flavour, follow the supplier's recommendation, then adjust to taste. For colour, add drop by drop until you get the shade. For preservatives, calculate based on final volume. For example, 100 L batch needs 15 g sodium benzoate and 20 g potassium sorbate.

A practical exercise: Make 20 L of orange soda. Start with 18 L water. Add 2 kg sugar (10 Brix). Add 20 g citric acid. Add 10 ml orange flavour. Add 2 g sodium benzoate and 3 g potassium sorbate. Add 2 ml yellow-orange colour. Mix well. Check Brix: should be 10. Check pH: should be around 3.0. Taste. Adjust if needed. Then bottle. Always sanitise bottles and caps. Keep a formulation sheet for every batch. That way you can repeat success.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Ingredients & Formulation for Soft Drinks in Africa

This practical reference consolidates the key formulation knowledge you need to run a soft drinks operation in Africa â from sourcing sweeteners and acidulants to hitting your target Brix and keeping shelf life under tropical conditions. It is written for the operator, the production manager, and the entrepreneur who needs to buy right, formulate consistently, and sell profitably. Every number here has a business consequence: a poorly calibrated Brix meter means a rejected batch; the wrong preservative dose means spoilage in a hot warehouse; a cheaper acidulant can save you money â or cost you a customer.

1. Sweeteners: The Biggest Cost Line

Sugar (sucrose) typically accounts for 30â50% of raw material cost in a carbonated soft drink. In most African markets, locally refined cane sugar is the default. High-Fructose Corn Syrup (HFCS) is rarely competitive in Africa because maize is usually more valuable as food and HFCS import logistics are expensive â but where it is available, HFCS-55 is roughly 1.1â1.3Ã sweeter than sucrose on a solids basis, so you use less. Artificial sweeteners (aspartame, acesulfame-K, sucralose, stevia) allow "zero sugar" or "low sugar" positioning, which matters in markets where regulators are taxing sugary drinks (e.g., South Africa's Health Promotion Levy, Kenya's excise on sugar content).

Practical rule: match your sweetener to your label claim and your tax band before you match it to your taste panel. A 10% sugar reduction that keeps you below a tax threshold can be worth more than a perfect flavour match.

2. Acidulants: Taste, Preservation, and Cost

Citric acid (E330) is the workhorse â around 60â70% of global beverage acidulant use. It gives a clean, fruity tartness and is available across Africa from fermentation plants (e.g., in Egypt, South Africa, Nigeria). Phosphoric acid (E338) is the cola signature: sharper, more "bite," and cheaper per unit of acid strength, which is why cola giants use it. Malic acid (E296) is sharper and more persistent than citric, often used in fruit-flavoured and sour confections; it is more expensive and less available locally.

Acidulants also lower pH, which is your first line of defence against spoilage. A pH below 4.0 (ideally 2.5â3.5 for carbonated drinks) suppresses most bacteria; only yeasts and moulds remain a threat, which is where preservatives come in.

3. Flavourings: Natural vs Synthetic

Natural flavourings (essential oils, fruit extracts, oleoresins) command a premium and support clean-label claims, but they are less stable under African heat and UV. Synthetic flavourings are cheaper, more consistent, and more heat-stable â the pragmatic choice for mass-market carbonates. For the growing premium and export segment, natural flavours plus a "no artificial flavours" claim can justify a 20â40% price premium. Buy from suppliers who can provide halal, kosher, and allergen documentation â this matters for export to the Middle East and for supermarket listings in South Africa and Kenya.

4. Colourants: Natural vs Artificial

Caramel colour (E150aâd) dominates colas and many dark drinks. It is cheap, stable, and produced in several African countries. Natural colours â anthocyanins from hibiscus (roselle), carotenoids from palm, beetroot red â are locally abundant and support "made in Africa" storytelling, but they fade under light and heat and can shift hue with pH. Artificial colours (e.g., tartrazine E102, sunset yellow E110) are cheap and stable but face mandatory warning labels in the EU and restrictions in some markets. If you export, check the destination's permitted list before you formulate.

5. Preservatives and Antioxidants

For carbonated drinks, the combination of low pH, COâ, and cold chain often makes preservatives unnecessary. For still drinks, juices, and syrups in tropical distribution, you need them. The standard tools are:

  • Potassium sorbate (E202) â effective against yeasts and moulds at pH < 4.5. Typical use: 200â500 mg/L (as sorbic acid).
  • Sodium benzoate (E211) â effective against bacteria and some yeasts at pH < 4.0. Typical use: 150â250 mg/L (as benzoic acid).
  • Combination â sorbate + benzoate gives broad-spectrum protection and is the industry standard for still soft drinks.
  • Antioxidants â ascorbic acid (vitamin C, E300) protects colours and flavours from oxidation; often used at 100â300 mg/L. It also allows a "with vitamin C" claim.

Critical legal point: maximum permitted levels differ by country. Always check your national food standards (e.g., KEBS in Kenya, NAFDAC in Nigeria, SABS/DoH in South Africa) before finalising a recipe.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Preservative and Acid Handling

Never mix sodium benzoate and potassium sorbate in concentrated form. When combined in high concentration at low pH, they can form benzoic acid crystals and, under some conditions, trace benzene â a known carcinogen. Always dilute each preservative separately in water before adding to the batch, and never add them to a hot syrup.

Phosphoric acid is corrosive. Concentrated phosphoric acid (75â85%) causes severe burns. Wear chemical splash goggles, nitrile gloves, and a face shield. Always add acid to water â never water to acid. Keep a running eyewash station within 10 metres of the dosing point. In many African plants, PPE compliance is the single biggest safety gap â enforce it.

Do not exceed legal maximum levels. Overdosing preservatives does not improve shelf life proportionally and can make your product non-compliant and unsaleable. Record every dose in your batch sheet.

6. Formulation Calculations and Brix Measurement

Brix (Â°Bx) is the percentage of dissolved solids by mass â essentially your sugar concentration. Getting it right is non-negotiable: it drives taste, mouthfeel, carbonation retention, and tax classification in some markets.

Key formula â syrup dilution:

Final Brix = (Simple syrup Brix Ã Syrup volume) Ã· (Syrup volume + Water volume)

Example: You have 100 L of 65 Â°Bx simple syrup and want a 12 Â°Bx final drink. You need to dilute to 12 Â°Bx. Required final volume = (65 Ã 100) Ã· 12 = 541.7 L. So add 441.7 L of treated water. In practice, you would prepare a "throw syrup" at higher Brix and dilute at the filler.

Measuring Brix: Use a calibrated refractometer (handheld for spot checks, inline for continuous production). Calibrate with distilled water at 20 Â°C daily. Temperature correction matters: a reading taken at 30 Â°C can be 0.5â1.0 Â°Bx off. In hot African plants, always apply the temperature correction table or use a refractometer with automatic temperature compensation (ATC).

Data Table 1: Typical Formulation Ranges for Carbonated Soft Drinks

Ingredient Typical Use Level Function Africa Sourcing Note
Sugar (sucrose) 8â12 Â°Brix Sweetness, body Local cane sugar in SA, Kenya, Nigeria, Egypt
Citric acid 0.05â0.25% Tartness, pH control Available from Egyptian and SA suppliers
Phosphoric acid 0.03â0.10% Cola bite, pH Mostly imported; buy in bulk drums
Caramel colour 0.05â0.30% Dark cola colour Produced in SA, Nigeria, Egypt
Potassium sorbate 200â500 mg/L Yeast/mould inhibition Imported; check KEBS/NAFDAC limits
Sodium benzoate 150â250 mg/L Bacterial inhibition Imported; never mix with sorbate concentrate
Ascorbic acid 100â300 mg/L Antioxidant, vitamin C claim Widely available; also locally produced

Source: Adapted from Ashurst, P.R. (ed.), Chemistry and Technology of Soft Drinks and Fruit Juices, 3rd ed., Wiley-Blackwell, 2016, and Codex Alimentarius General Standard for Food Additives (GSFA) online database, FAO/WHO, 2023.

Data Table 2: Brix Targets and Temperature Correction Quick Guide

Product Type Target Â°Brix Reading at 30 Â°C (approx.) Correction to 20 Â°C
Cola / carbonated 10.5â11.5 10.3â11.3 Add ~0.2 Â°Bx
Orange / fruit carbonate 11.0â12.5 10.8â12.3 Add ~0.2 Â°Bx
Still juice drink (10% juice) 8.0â10.0 7.8â9.8 Add ~0.2 Â°Bx
Concentrate / squash 55â65 54.5â64.5 Add ~0.5 Â°Bx
Energy drink 12.0â14.0 11.8â13.8 Add ~0.2 Â°Bx

Source: Brix temperature correction values derived from ICUMSA (International Commission for Uniform Methods of Sugar Analysis) Specification and Standard SPS-3, 1994, and practical calibration data from ATAGO refractometer manuals (ATAGO Co. Ltd., Japan, 2020).

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Calibrate your refractometer daily with distilled water at 20 Â°C â record the reading in the batch log.
  2. Confirm your target Â°Brix against the product spec before mixing; never eyeball the sugar.
  3. Check pH after adding acidulant â target 2.5â3.5 for carbonated, 3.0â4.0 for still drinks.
  4. Dilute preservatives separately before adding to syrup; never mix sorbate and benzoate concentrates.
  5. Verify legal limits for preservatives, colours, and sweeteners against your national standard (KEBS, NAFDAC, SABS, etc.).
  6. Wear PPE (goggles, gloves, face shield) when handling phosphoric acid or concentrated preservatives.
  7. Record every ingredient weight and batch number â traceability is required for supermarket and export listings.
  8. Taste-test against your gold standard before filling; small Brix or pH drifts are cheaper to fix in the tank than in the market.

Further Reading

  • FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius â General Standard for Food Additives (GSFA) Online Database â free, official, covers permitted additives and maximum levels.
  • WHO â Guidelines on Non-Sugar Sweeteners (2023) â free PDF, essential for zero-sugar product development.
  • Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) â free access to Kenya's beverage standards and additive limits.
  • NAFDAC (Nigeria) â free regulatory guidance for food and beverage registration and additive limits.
  • South African Bureau of Standards (SABS) â free catalogue of SANS standards for soft drinks and labelling.

This module is part of the RISE AFRICA Skills programme. Always verify local regulations before commercial production. Formulation is a business decision â every gram you save or waste shows up on your P&L.

quiz.q: What is the typical Brix range for a regular soft drink?
quiz.explanation: Most soft drinks are formulated at 10â12 Brix for optimal sweetness and mouthfeel.

quiz.q: Which sweetener is about 200 times sweeter than sugar?
quiz.explanation: Aspartame is approximately 200 times sweeter than sucrose, so only a tiny amount is needed.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid combining sodium benzoate with vitamin C?
options: B) It forms benzene, a carcinogen
quiz.explanation: Sodium benzoate and ascorbic acid can react to form benzene, which is harmful.

quiz.q: Which acid is most commonly used in cola drinks?
quiz.explanation: Phosphoric acid gives cola its characteristic tang and is the traditional acidulant for colas.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended dosage of sodium benzoate in soft drinks?
quiz.explanation: Typical usage is 150â200 mg per litre, depending on local regulations.

quiz.q: Which natural colourant is commonly used for cola drinks?
quiz.explanation: Caramel colour, made by heating sugar, gives colas their dark brown colour.

quiz.q: What is the function of an emulsifier in flavour addition?
options: B) To help oil-based flavours mix with water
quiz.explanation: Emulsifiers like gum arabic allow flavour oils to disperse evenly in the water-based drink.

quiz.q: Which of these is a natural sweetener with a bitter aftertaste?
quiz.explanation: Stevia is natural but often has a bitter or licorice-like aftertaste.

quiz.q: What pH range is typical for most soft drinks?
quiz.explanation: Soft drinks are usually acidic, with pH between 2.5 and 3.5 for preservation and taste.

quiz.q: Which preservative works best at pH below 4.5?
quiz.explanation: Sodium benzoate is most effective in acidic conditions (pH < 4.5).

quiz.q: How much sugar is needed for 100 L of 10 Brix solution?
quiz.explanation: 10 Brix means 10 g sugar per 100 g solution; for 100 L (approx 100 kg), that's 10 kg sugar.

quiz.q: Which artificial colour is also known as Yellow 5?
quiz.explanation: Tartrazine is Yellow 5, a common synthetic yellow dye.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of ascorbic acid in soft drinks?
quiz.explanation: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) acts as an antioxidant, protecting colours and flavours from oxidation.

quiz.q: Which flavour compound is responsible for vanilla aroma?
quiz.explanation: Ethyl vanillin is a synthetic vanilla flavour, stronger than natural vanillin.

quiz.q: How should you add phosphoric acid to water?
quiz.explanation: Always add acid to water to prevent violent reactions and splashing.

quiz.q: What is the typical usage rate for a flavour concentrate?
quiz.explanation: Most flavour concentrates are used at 0.1â0.5% of the final beverage volume.

quiz.q: Which of these is a natural red colourant?
quiz.explanation: Anthocyanins from berries or red cabbage give red to purple colours.

quiz.q: What is the maximum allowed level of Tartrazine in many soft drinks?
quiz.explanation: Many countries limit Tartrazine to 100 mg per litre in beverages.

quiz.q: Which two preservatives are commonly used together?
options: A) Sodium benzoate and potassium sorbate
C) Citric acid and ascorbic acid
quiz.explanation: Sodium benzoate and potassium sorbate are often combined for broad-spectrum protection.

quiz.q: What does a refractometer measure?
quiz.explanation: A refractometer measures Brix, the percentage of dissolved solids (mostly sugar).

quiz.q: Which acid is found naturally in apples?
quiz.explanation: Malic acid is the predominant acid in apples, giving a smooth sour taste.

quiz.q: How much aspartame is needed to replace 100 g of sugar per litre?
quiz.explanation: Aspartame is 200 times sweeter, so 100 g / 200 = 0.5 g per litre.

quiz.q: What is the role of EDTA in soft drinks?
quiz.explanation: EDTA chelates metal ions, preventing them from causing off-flavours or colour changes.

quiz.q: Which of these is a synthetic flavour?
quiz.explanation: Limonene is a synthetic or isolated citrus flavour compound, not a natural extract.

quiz.q: Why should artificial colours be dissolved in a small amount of water first?
quiz.explanation: Pre-dissolving prevents concentrated dye from causing uneven colour spots.

quiz.q: What is the typical pH of a non-acidic drink where benzoate is ineffective?
quiz.explanation: Sodium benzoate works poorly above pH 4.5, so it is ineffective in low-acid drinks.

quiz.q: Which ingredient adds mouthfeel and body to a soft drink?
quiz.explanation: Sugar provides sweetness and also contributes to the drink's body and mouthfeel.

quiz.q: What is the recommended storage for natural colours?
quiz.explanation: Natural colours are perishable and should be refrigerated to extend shelf life.

quiz.q: How much potassium sorbate is typically used per litre?
quiz.explanation: Potassium sorbate is usually used at 200â300 mg per litre for preservation.

quiz.q: Which of these is a step in formulating a 20 L batch of orange soda?
quiz.explanation: Always measure Brix after mixing all ingredients to ensure target sweetness.
